prompt: A number is called *good* if it can be written as the sum of the squares of three consecutive positive integers. A number is called *excellent* if it can be written as the sum of the squares of four consecutive positive integers. (For instance, $14=1^2+2^2+3^2$ is good and $30=1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2$ is excellent.) A good number $G$ is called *splendid* if there exists an excellent number $E$ such that $3G-E=2025$. If the sum of all splendid numbers is $S$, find the remainder when $S$ is divided by $1000$.

Call an arrangement of $n$ not necessarily distinct nonnegative integers in a circle *wholesome* when, for any subset of the integers such that no pair of them is adjacent in the circle, their average is an integer. Over all wholesome arrangements of $n$ integers where at least two of them are distinct, let $M(n)$ denote the smallest possible value for the maximum of the integers in the arrangement. What is the largest integer $n<2023$ such that $M(n+1)$ is strictly greater than $M(n)$?
What is the smallest possible sum of six distinct positive integers for which the sum of any five of them is prime?

You play a game where you and an adversarial opponent take turns writing down positive integers on a chalkboard; the only condition is that, if $m$ and $n$ are written consecutively on the board, $\gcd(m,n)$ must be squarefree. If your objective is to make sure as many integers as possible that are strictly less than $404$ end up on the board (and your opponent is trying to minimize this quantity), how many more such integers can you guarantee will eventually be written on the board if you get to move first as opposed to when your opponent gets to move first?
How many positive integers $n\le\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,100)$ have the property that $n$ gives different remainders when divided by each of $2,3,\dots,100$?

Define $f(n)$ to be the smallest integer such that for every positive divisor $d\mid n$, either $n\mid d^d$ or $d^d\mid n^{f(n)}$. How many positive integers $b<1000$ which are not squarefree satisfy the equation $f(2023)\cdot f(b)=f(2023b)$?

solutions.title: Closed form for $f$
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** If $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$ and $g(n)=\min_ip_i^{e_i}$ (the smallest prime-power component), then $f(n)=\dfrac n{g(n)}$.

*Lower bound.* Let $p_k^{e_k}=g(n)$ and $d=n/g(n)$. Then $p_k\nmid d$, so $n\nmid d^d$; hence we need $d^d\mid n^{f}$. For $i\ne k$ this reads $e_i d\le e_if$, so $f\ge d=n/g(n)$.

*Upper bound* (take $f=n/g$). Let $d\mid n$. (1) If some prime $p_j\mid n$ does not divide $d$, then $d\mid d_j:=n/p_j^{e_j}\le n/g$, so $d^d\mid d_j^{d_j}$, which has $p_j$-exponent $0$ and $p_\ell$-exponent $e_\ell d_j\le e_\ell n/g$ for $\ell\ne j$; thus $d^d\mid n^{n/g}$. (2) If $d$ contains every prime of $n$, say $d=\prod p_i^{a_i}$ with $1\le a_i\le e_i$: either $e_i\le a_id$ for all $i$ (then $n\mid d^d$), or some $e_k>a_kd$; then $d<e_k/a_k$ and for every $\ell$, $a_\ell d<\frac{a_\ell e_k}{a_k}\le e_\ell\cdot e_k\le e_\ell\frac{n}{g}$ because for $n$ with at least two prime factors $\frac ng\ge\sqrt n\ge\sqrt2\cdot2^{e_k/2}\ge e_k$ (and prime powers are immediate). So $d^d\mid n^{n/g}$. $\square$

**Reduction.** $f(m)f(n)=f(mn)\iff\frac{mn}{g(m)g(n)}=\frac{mn}{g(mn)}\iff g(mn)=g(m)g(n)$. With $2023=7\cdot17^2$, $g(2023)=7$, so we need $g(2023b)=7\,g(b)$.

Both $g(b)$ and $g(2023b)$ are prime powers, so $g(b)=7^j$ with $j\ge1$ ($b>1$). If $j\ge2$ every other prime-power component of $b$ exceeds $49$, forcing $b\ge49\cdot50>1000$ unless $b$ is a power of $7$; but for $b=49,343$ one finds $g(2023b)=289\ne7g(b)$. So $g(b)=7$, $b=7a$ with $7\nmid a$ and $g(2023b)=49$: since $2023b=7^2\cdot17^2\cdot a$, all prime-power components of $a$ other than the $17$-part must be $\ge49$. If $17\mid a$ then $a=17a'$ with $a'<9$ and $a'$ would have to be $1$ (components $\ge49$), giving the squarefree $b=119$; so $17\nmid a$. Then $a<143$ is a single prime power $\ge49$; for $b=7a$ not to be squarefree $a$ must have exponent $\ge2$: $a\in\{64,81,121,125,128\}$.

Hence $b=448,567,847,875,896$: **5** values.

**Answer: 5**

prompt: Let $S_0=0$, $S_1=1$, and for $n\ge2$ let $S_n=S_{n-1}+5S_{n-2}$. What is the sum of the five smallest primes $p$ such that $p\mid S_{p-1}$?

solutions.title: Binomial formula and Legendre symbol
solutions.body:
With $\alpha,\beta=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{21}}2$ (roots of $x^2=x+5$), $S_n=\frac{\alpha^n-\beta^n}{\sqrt{21}}$, and expanding the binomials,
$$2^{n-1}S_n=\sum_{k\ge0}\binom n{2k+1}21^k.$$
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $p\nmid21$, and $\lambda=21^{(p-1)/2}\equiv\left(\frac{21}p\right)=\pm1$. Mod $p$ only the binomials $\binom p{p}=1$ (top term) survive in $2^{p-1}S_p$, and Fermat gives $S_p\equiv\lambda$. For $n=p+1$: $\binom{p+1}1\equiv1$ and $\binom{p+1}{p}21^{(p-1)/2}\equiv\lambda$, so $2^pS_{p+1}\equiv1+\lambda$, i.e. $S_{p+1}\equiv\frac{1+\lambda}2$.

From $S_{p+1}=S_p+5S_{p-1}$: $5S_{p-1}\equiv\frac{1+\lambda}2-\lambda=\frac{1-\lambda}2$. For $p\ne5$ this is $\equiv0$ iff $\lambda=1$. So (for $p\nmid2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$) $p\mid S_{p-1}\iff\left(\frac{21}p\right)=1$.

Small primes directly: $S_1=1$, $S_2=1$, $S_4=11$, $S_6=96$, so $2,3,5,7$ fail. Among larger primes, $21$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$ exactly for $17$ ($4\equiv21$), $37$ ($13^2\equiv21$), $41$ ($12^2\equiv21$), $43$ ($8^2\equiv21$), $47$ ($16^2\equiv21$), while for $11,13,19,23,29,31$ it is a non-residue. (Equivalently, by quadratic reciprocity $\left(\frac{21}p\right)=\left(\frac p3\right)\left(\frac p7\right)$.)

The five smallest such primes are $17,37,41,43,47$, with sum $185$.

**Answer: 185**
